# Bojjhaṅga Saṁyutta (SN 46)

**ID:** SN 46
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Bojjhaṅga Saṁyutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Linked Discourses on the Awakening Factors
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/sn46
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0305m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bojjhaṅgasaṁyutta* (SN 46, PTS S V 63–140) is the forty-sixth collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, containing discourses on the seven factors of awakening (*bojjhaṅga*, a compound of *bodhi* and *aṅga*) [Bodhi 2003; Analayo 2003; Nguyen Van Thuong]. In the SuttaCentral division, the section encompasses 184 discourses grouped under 38 suttas, focusing explicitly on meditative cultivation rather than general path descriptions [SuttaCentral]. While later commentarial and Abhidhamma traditions often interpret these factors by analogy with *jhāna* factors (*jhānaṅga*) or assign them strictly to supramundane consciousness, in the discourses they operate as mental faculties developed through practice [Bodhi 2003]. Throughout the saṁyutta, the seven awakening factors are repeatedly presented as diametrically opposed antidotes to the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and as vehicles for the abandonment of craving (*taṇhā*) and the higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṁyojana*) [SuttaCentral; Gaffney 2003; Analayo 2003]. Prominent discourses include the *Aggi-sutta* (SN 46.53), which uses the metaphor of fire to show how mindfulness balances activating factors (investigation, energy, joy) against sluggishness and calming factors (tranquillity, concentration, equanimity) against restlessness [Analayo 2018; Wen]; the *Pariyāya-sutta* (SN 46.52), which outlines internal and external applications for the factors [Analayo 2018]; the *Kuṇḍaliya-sutta* (SN 46.6) on sense restraint [Wen]; and discourses on the recitation of awakening factors to inspire and relieve the sick (e.g., SN 46.14 to Mahākassapa) [SuttaCentral; Salguero 2017; Analayo 2016].

SuttaCentral lists 38 discourses in this saṁyutta with parallels across Buddhist canons, especially within the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (SĀ / T 99; 28 parallels), alongside texts in the *Madhyamāgama* (MĀ 58), *Ekottarikāgama* (EĀ 39.7), individual translations (T 38), and Sanskrit manuscript fragments (SF 124, SF 186) [SuttaCentral]. SN 46.14 has a Tibetan translation in the Kangyur (D 40 / Q 756), as well as related fragments in Sanskrit and Old Uighur [Salguero 2017; Analayo 2016]. DharmaNexus confirms substantial cross-linguistic alignment with Chinese T 99, T 26, and T 125, the Tibetan *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D 4094), and Sanskrit sūtra fragments including the *Arthaviniścayasūtra* and *Nidānasaṃyukta* [DharmaNexus]. Internally, DharmaNexus records extensive text reuse between SN 46 and the *Magga Saṁyutta* (SN 45), the *Ānāpāna Saṁyutta* (SN 54), multiple divisions of the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 5, AN 10, AN 6, AN 4, AN 3, AN 1), the *Ānāpānassati Sutta* (MN 118), and exegeses in the *Visuddhimagga* and *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
